fr:title.text: ▷ as a Later Modality from Tiny Strings

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: ▷ as a Later Modality from Tiny Strings

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A candidate later modality ▷ for the Dependent Lambek Calculus, built directly out of the "amazing right adjoints" to character derivatives that already live on the brzozowski branch. Sister proposal to sss-00AC, which makes ▷ a primitive guard on μ and a synonym for - \mathbin {\htmlStyle {display:inline-block;transform:rotate(180deg);}{\multimap }} \textrm {char}\, c; this tree takes the orthogonal route of constructing ▷ from the existing amazing-right-adjoint operations indexed over strings.

fr:title.text: Recap: amazing right adjoint to a single character

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Recap: amazing right adjoint to a single character

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Recall from Grammar/Derivative/Base.agda that for a character c the right Brzozowski derivative is the linear residual D_l\, A\, c \;=\; A \mathbin {\htmlStyle {display:inline-block;transform:rotate(180deg);}{\multimap }} \texttt {"}c\texttt {"}. The "amazing right adjoint" — the further right adjoint, in the sense of the tiny-object story — is given by
with the symmetric variant
when the character sits at the end of a string. These already exist in the codebase as √l c A and √r c A, with √l-app witnessing the counit D_l\, (\sqrt {c}\, A)\, c \vdash A.

The amazing-right-adjoint construction goes through for any tiny object, not only single characters. In the grammar setting strings are tiny: an inhabited string is a finite product of literal grammars under \otimes , and \texttt {"}c\texttt {"} \otimes - preserves all colimits, so iterating gives a left adjoint \texttt {String}\, w \otimes - with both adjoints on the right.

Notation. For a non-empty string w, write \sqrt [w]{A} for the right-adjoint indexed over w; concretely \sqrt [w]{A} \;=\; (\texttt {String}\, w \otimes \top ) \Rightarrow (\texttt {String}\, w \otimes A) on the left-handed side, with the obvious right-handed dual. The single-character √l c A is the special case w = [c].

Define \rhd A \;:=\; \mathchoice {\textstyle \And _{{\mathopen {}\left (w \in \texttt {String}^{+}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \And _{{\mathopen {}\left (w \in \texttt {String}^{+}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \And _{{\mathopen {}\left (w \in \texttt {String}^{+}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \And _{{\mathopen {}\left (w \in \texttt {String}^{+}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\sqrt [w]{A}. A point of ▷ A is a coherent family: for every non-empty string w, a witness that consuming a w-prefix exposes an A. The indexing is by all non-empty strings simultaneously, so the modality is character-agnostic in the same sense as classical guarded type theory's ▷, while being grounded in concrete suffix-extraction at every non-empty depth.
Two design questions are baked into the definition.

html:ul.html:li: Side. We pick the left-handed \sqrt [w]{}, which encodes "any proper suffix"; the right-handed choice gives "any proper prefix". They are symmetric and either could serve. A genuinely two-sided ▷ encoding "any proper substring" is the natural next target — see TODOs below.

Why non-empty. Empty w would give \sqrt [\epsilon ]{A} \cong A, collapsing \rhd A \vdash A into a strict identity and killing Löb. Restricting to non-empty strings keeps the modality genuinely "later".

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The candidate is only useful if it has the structural rules of a later modality. Three properties to check.

html:ol.html:li: Next. A canonical map \mathsf {next} : A \vdash \rhd A. Heuristic construction: for each non-empty w the component should factor through the strength of \sqrt [w]{} on A, packaging the universal property of the amazing right adjoint with the splitting \texttt {String}\, w \otimes \top \vdash \texttt {String}\, w \otimes A that already holds when A is global.

Functoriality and \sqrt {}-applicativity. Since ▷ is a \And -indexed limit of right adjoints it is automatically a right adjoint, hence preserves limits. The genuinely calculus-specific check is the interaction with \otimes : do we get \rhd (A \otimes B) \vdash \rhd A \otimes \rhd B, or its dual, in a way that lets later-style applicative bookkeeping go through?

Löb induction. (\rhd A \vdash A) \;\Rightarrow \; (\top \vdash A). Conjectural argument sketch: from \rhd A \vdash A and next build \rhd A \vdash \rhd A as a \sqrt [w]{}-coalgebra in each component; uniqueness on each component forces the global fixed point, and the limit of "the unique fixed point" is the unique fixed point of the limit. The character-by-character flavor of this matches the well-founded-on-string-length argument used in sss-00A8 to build the Brzozowski parser, suggesting that Löb here is in fact the same principle, repackaged.

Once the suffix-flavored ▷ above is established, the natural generalisation drops the "at the start" or "at the end" constraint. fr:title.text: Resolution: next is structure, not a theorem

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Resolution: next is structure, not a theorem

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The diagram chase does not go through for arbitrary grammars — the verification check anticipated above fails. next is not derivable from the indexed-product definition of ▷ alone; it requires extra structure on A.

Max's framing. Presheaves on (\texttt {String}, \text {suffix-order}) are precisely \Box -coalgebras over families. The map next : A ⊢ ▷ A is the coalgebra structure, not a global term. So instead of postulating it (or holding it open as a hole), package it as a record:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: record IsCoalgebra (A : Grammar ℓA) : Type ℓA where field next : A ⊢ ▷ A
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The canonical example is ⊤-IsCoalgebra: ⊤ is suffix-closed because any suffix of a ⊤-parse is a ⊤-parse. This lives in Grammar/Later/Coalgebra.agda on the guarded branch of gsa-brzozowski.

html:ul.html:li: Grammar/Later/Base.agda now compiles without --allow-unsolved-metas — the held-open next hole is gone.
Löb (sss-00BE) goes through unchanged: the obstruction to next does not block Löb, because Löb is proven directly by well-founded recursion on string length and never invokes a global next.

This is the same shape of design discovery as Cass's recursive-coalgebra framework: well-foundedness + recursion lives on coalgebra structures, not on bare grammars. The connection is made explicit in the recursive-coalgebra synthesis — next is the coalgebra structure that feeds a c2a-morphism.

fr:title.text: Open recursion for grammars: the contextual Löb rule

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Open recursion for grammars: the contextual Löb rule

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The closed Löb principle {\mathopen {}\left (\rhd A \vdash A\right )\mathclose {}} \Rightarrow {\mathopen {}\left (\top \vdash A\right )\mathclose {}} for the constructed \rhd builds a global term \top \vdash A. That is enough to define a closed recursive grammar, but not to define a recursive parser in a context — parametrised combinators, threaded accumulators, precedence-indexed families. This note records the open (contextual) form as precise entailments, and pins the exact side condition, sharpening sss-00BD's discovery that \mathsf {next} is coalgebra structure rather than a theorem.

The rule. Internalise closed Löb at the exponential \Gamma \Rightarrow A. From \rhd {\mathopen {}\left (\Gamma \Rightarrow A\right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \Gamma \Rightarrow A closed Löb gives \top \vdash \Gamma \Rightarrow A, i.e. \Gamma \vdash A. Uncurrying the premise, open guarded recursion is

The recursive call is the delayed \rhd {\mathopen {}\left (\Gamma \Rightarrow A\right )\mathclose {}}; the hypotheses in \Gamma are available now. At \Gamma = \top it collapses (\top \Rightarrow A \cong A) back to closed Löb \rhd A \vdash A. Note \And is a type former and \vdash the hom, so the premise is the single entailment above — not \Gamma conjoined with a judgement.

The catch: firing the call. To apply \rhd {\mathopen {}\left (\Gamma \Rightarrow A\right )\mathclose {}} you must first produce \rhd \Gamma and use later-applicativity. That needs \mathsf {next}_\Gamma : \Gamma \vdash \rhd \Gamma , which by sss-00BD is not free: it is exactly an \mathsf {IsCoalgebra}\,\Gamma structure, i.e. a suffix-closed \Gamma . So the whole content of "open" reduces to one condition:

html:blockquote.html:p: Open recursion over a context \Gamma is available iff \Gamma carries \mathsf {next}_\Gamma , i.e. iff \Gamma is suffix-closed (a \rhd -coalgebra).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two sources of the step. The delayed argument the recursive call consumes can arrive two ways.

html:ul.html:li: By \mathsf {next} — when \Gamma is a coalgebra. Constant grammars \Delta S, the unit \top (the canonical \top -coalgebra of sss-00BD), and any \rhd B are suffix-closed, so \mathsf {next} exists on them.

By consumption — the parsing-specific route, needing no \mathsf {next}. If the recursive occurrence sits behind A \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} with A positive (A\,\varepsilon = \varnothing : no empty parse), then {\mathopen {}\left (A \otimes X\right )\mathclose {}}\,w depends on X only at proper suffixes of w; hence A \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} factors through \rhd , and \mu X.\,\mathrm {base} \oplus A \otimes X is a guarded fixed point. The \otimes pays the step that \mathsf {next} would.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: This is the precise form of "guardedness by consuming a token": \texttt {"}c\texttt {"} \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} is the single-character \rhd of sss-00AC, and A \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (-\right )\mathclose {}} for positive A is its many-step generalisation.

html:ol.html:li: Kleene iteration. \mathsf {iter}\,A := \mu X.\, I \oplus A \otimes X for positive A. Open in the grammar parameter A, which is substituted and sits inside the guard — no \mathsf {next} needed. Cf. greedy Kleene star.

Left folds (\mathsf {chainl1}). Parse p\,{\mathopen {}\left (\mathit {op}\,p\right )\mathclose {}}^{\ast } threading an accumulator a : \Delta {\mathopen {}\left (\mathrm {Tree}\right )\mathclose {}}. The accumulator lives in a constant grammar — a coalgebra — so the contextual rule applies with \Gamma = \Delta {\mathopen {}\left (\mathrm {Tree}\right )\mathclose {}}.

Pratt / precedence climbing. \mathsf {pratt} : \Delta \mathbb {N} \vdash \mathrm {Parser}\,E with \mathsf {pratt}\,p recursing at a fresh level p'. This is exactly the precedence-indexed Löb family of sss-00BZ item 1, \rhd {\mathopen {}\left (\Pi p.\,\mathrm {Parser}\,E\right )\mathclose {}} \vdash \Pi p.\,\mathrm {Parser}\,E; the context \Delta \mathbb {N} is constant, hence a coalgebra, so \rhd distributes through the \Pi .

Attribute grammars. Inherited attributes flow into the recursive calls — the threaded context \Gamma ; synthesized attributes are the result A. The rule applies exactly when the inherited attribute is suffix-closed, which is automatic for position-independent (constant) attributes. A position-varying inherited attribute — a grammar indexed by the input already consumed — is not a coalgebra; this is precisely the boundary of genuinely context-sensitive parsing.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The dividing line. Substituted parameters, constant threads, and \rhd -guarded self-references are all coalgebras, so essentially every standard combinator is open-recursible without the applicative structure of \rhd . The one thing genuinely ruled out is transporting a position-dependent grammar down into the recursion — an inherited attribute indexed by the consumed prefix — which is where sss-00BD's missing \mathsf {next} actually bites.

Semantically this is nothing new beyond sss-00A8: the same well-founded-on-string-length induction that proves closed Löb relativises to any coalgebra context \Gamma , and that relativisation is the rule above.

fr:title.text: 1. Pratt grammars parametric in precedence and fixity

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: 1. Pratt grammars parametric in precedence and fixity

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The generic parser in Examples.PrattRDLaterGen fixes one precedence level and right-associativity. To carry precedence p \in \{0, \dots , N\} and per-operator fixity, three viable encodings:

html:ul.html:li: Stratified inductive grammar. Index the grammar functor by precedence level: E_p := E_{p-1} \mid E_{p-1}\, op_p\, E_p (right-assoc) or with iteration for left-assoc. This is a mutually indexed inductive — define the functor F : \mathrm {Fin}\,N \to \mathrm {Functor}\,(\mathrm {Fin}\,N) and take \mu F. The parser becomes a finite tuple of mutually recursive Löb-fixed parsers, one per level.

Single grammar, precedence-indexed parser. Keep the grammar flat (E := A \mid A\, \mathrm {Op}\, E) and let the parser enforce precedence at parse time. Parser type: \mathrm {Lev} \to \mathsf {string} \vdash \mathsf {Parser}\,E. Löb-fix the whole family: \triangleright (\forall p.\,\mathsf {Parser}\,E) \vdash \forall p.\,\mathsf {Parser}\,E. This needs \triangleright to distribute through \Pi , which is standard in guarded type theory and should hold for the left-handed later modality in use here.

Per-operator threshold. Each operator carries (lbp, rbp). The parser checks \mathit {lbp}(\mathit {op}) > \mathrm {minPrec} and recurses with \mathit {rbp}(\mathit {op}). Right-assoc: \mathit {rbp} = \mathit {lbp} - 1; left-assoc: \mathit {rbp} = \mathit {lbp}. The left-assoc case requires the "loop" rather than "fold" recursion shape — see item 6 for the substring-modality angle.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Spec extension:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
record OpInfo : Type where field prec : ℕ rightAssoc : Bool
record PrattSpec : Type₁ where field AI : Type ℓ-zero ; isSetAI : isSet AI OI : Type ℓ-zero ; isSetOI : isSet OI opInfo : OI → OpInfo
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The hard part isn't the spec — it's the parser body. The Löb-fixed precedence-indexed family is probably the cleanest path; the stratified inductive view is the cleanest grammar-level description.
The current tests assert acceptP w ≡ true via Bool-valued acceptance because building the full parse witness blows up term size. Sources of the blowup:

html:ul.html:li: Splittings: every \otimes carries a (w_1, w_2, p : w \equiv w_1 ++ w_2) record. Compositions stack these records.
Inductive grammar \mu F uses liftG/lowerG wrappers that don't reduce away under DSL combinators.
The Maybe⊗r, fmap, ⊕-elim chains produce nested case analyses that normalise to large terms even on small inputs.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Candidate fixes, roughly cheapest first:

html:ul.html:li: Bool-valued acceptance is sufficient most of the time. The current trick.

Structural test predicate. Define matchTree : Expr → BoolTree (a flat ADT mirroring the parse shape), recurse on the recognized witness, and compare against an expected BoolTree. This sidesteps splittings entirely. The "compare" reduces to Bool equality on a tree of tags.

Rewrite rules for monoidal laws. Declare \otimes -unit, \otimes -assoc, and \otimes -symmetry-equations as BUILTIN REWRITE, so that the elaborator collapses chains of ⊗-assoc⁻ ∘g ⊗-assoc during normalisation. Cubical paths complicate this — would need either eq-style rewrites (cf. AsEquality port) or careful `--rewriting` discipline.

Specialised evaluator. Write \mathsf {eval} : (\mathsf {string} \vdash \mathsf {Maybe}\,(A \otimes \mathsf {string})) \to \mathrm {List}\,\mathrm {Sym} \to \mathrm {Maybe}\,(\mathrm {AST}\,A \times \mathrm {List}\,\mathrm {Sym}) that interprets each DSL combinator on flat data structures (no splittings, no LiftG). Prove a correctness theorem once; then tests use eval for speed.

Two-tier opaque/transparent layers. The current eval-parser unfolds everything; consider a finer-grained eval-parser-tree marker that unfolds only the structural spine. The cubical paths in splittings would stay sealed.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The structural test predicate is probably the highest leverage — it captures the parse shape (which is what tests want to assert) without ever materialising splittings.
Two questions: can we do lexing in the DSL, and what's the ergonomic way to write test inputs.

In-DSL lexing. A lexer is a parser whose target grammar is a token stream. Building one in the DSL is mechanically possible: Kleene-*, \oplus , and disjunction are available. A LexerSpec record would carry per-token regexes plus a priority order (for longest-match / first-match disambiguation). Output: \mathsf {string}_\mathrm {raw} \vdash \mathsf {Maybe}\,(\mathrm {TokenList} \otimes \varepsilon ). The cost is non-trivial — whitespace handling, keyword tables, longest-match, error recovery — and offers no real benefit over an ordinary Agda function unless we want to reason semantically about lexer correctness in the same vocabulary as the parser.
Ergonomic test inputs. The pragmatic answer is to keep lexing external: an Agda function
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: lex : Agda.Builtin.String.String → List Sym lex s = lex' (primStringToList s) where lex' : List Char → List Sym lex' [] = [] lex' ('a' ∷ cs) = ⌜a⌝ ∷ lex' cs lex' ('+' ∷ cs) = ⌜+⌝ ∷ lex' cs ...
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Then acceptExpr (lex "a+b*a") typechecks and reduces identically to the hand-written a ∷ +t ∷ b ∷ *t ∷ a ∷ []. For multi-character tokens (let, =, identifiers), the lexer needs maximal-munch and a keyword table — also routine in plain Agda.

For the further-out goal of writing \texttt {"let x = 5 in x"} directly: combine the lexer above with a preprocessor that recognises identifiers and literals as token-with- payload. The token type extends from a plain enum to a tagged sum: Token = LET ∣ IN ∣ EQ ∣ IDENT String ∣ INT ℕ, and the parser's alphabet becomes this richer type (with appropriate isSet proof, e.g. via a retract through \mathbb {N} \uplus \mathrm {String} \uplus \mathrm {Fin}\,k).

Semantic bridging. If desired, prove \mathsf {lex}^* \equiv \mathsf {lex}_\mathrm {DSL} as a refinement theorem connecting the external lexer to an in-DSL specification. This pays for itself if you want end-to-end soundness statements ("parse of "a+b" produces this AST"), but isn't needed for the test-ergonomics use case alone.

The current type \mathsf {Parser}\,A = \mathsf {Maybe}\,(A \otimes \mathsf {string}) doesn't promise that nothing only fires on strings outside the language. A few ways to fix this in the type signature:

html:ul.html:li: Decision-procedure parsers. Replace the type with \mathsf {Parser}_!\,A = \mathsf {string} \cong (A \otimes \mathsf {string}) \oplus \mathrm {NoParse}_A where the right summand captures negative information ("no prefix of the input is in A"). NoParse is the tricky bit — it might be definable as \mathsf {string} \multimap (A \to \bot ) or via decidability witnesses.
Refinement-typed parsers. Bundle the morphism with its soundness/completeness proofs:
html:ul.html:pre: record CompleteParser (A : Grammar ℓ) : Type where field parse : string ⊢ Maybe (A ⊗ string) sound : ∀ w → parse w ≡ inl r → ⟨A w⟩ on (r.fst.fst) complete : ∀ w → parse w ≡ inr _ → ¬ ∃ accepting-split-of w
html:ul.html:li: Unambiguous-grammar route. For unambiguous LL(k) grammars, derive the parser directly from a grammar-equivalence proof \mathsf {string} \cong A \oplus \neg A. The Examples.BinOp.LL⟨1⟩ family already has this structure for LL(1); generalising the technique would be the principled route.
Total-by-construction. Index parsers by their language denotation; require that combinators preserve a "completeness" predicate (cf. item 5).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The cheapest practical move is the refinement-typed bundle — add soundness and completeness as ancillary fields that parser combinators thread through automatically. The unambiguous-grammar route is the most principled but requires a much heavier metatheory investment.
Danielsson's Total Parser Combinators (ICFP'10) builds total parsers in Agda by:

html:ol.html:li: Indexing parsers by the language they recognise (\mathsf {Parser}\,A\,L produces values of type A from inputs in L).
Encoding "consumes at least one token" as a type-level annotation (\mathit {null} vs \mathit {nonNull}) so that the combinator algebra rejects unproductive recursion.
Using coinductive/depth-indexed types so that the parser is total by construction.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Mapping to dependent Lambek:

html:ul.html:li: Language indexing is automatic — the grammar A is the language denotation, baked into the parser type.

Consumption annotation maps to the later modality: ▷-app-NE-keep-⌈⌉ requires a non-empty static prefix, which is exactly Danielsson's "must consume". So \triangleright on the left-handed modality corresponds to Danielsson's "delayed parser, productive after consumption".

Productivity / totality maps to Löb induction: the fixed-point combinator lob is well-defined precisely because every recursive call passes through \triangleright , mirroring how Danielsson's coinductive parsers are productive because every corecursive call passes through the depth annotation.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: So yes, the techniques apply, and the correspondence is reasonably tight: \triangleright \leftrightarrow consumption annotation, lob \leftrightarrow guarded fixed point, fixP \leftrightarrow fix on coinductive parsers. Direct adaptations worth importing:

html:ul.html:li: The "null"/"nonNull" distinction would let us forbid fixP id-style nonsense at the type level.

Danielsson's algebraic laws ((p₁ ⊕ p₂) ⊕ p₃ ≡ p₁ ⊕ (p₂ ⊕ p₃), left/right unit, etc.) transfer to our combinators essentially verbatim, and proving them would let combinator-level rewriting drive test-time normalisation (cf. item 2).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Current modalities: \triangleright (left-handed, consumes a non-empty prefix) and \triangleright ^r (right-handed, consumes a non-empty suffix). A natural third option is the substring modality \triangleright _\mathrm {sub}, expressing "later on any proper substring". sss-00B9 already sketches one shape for this; below fleshes out the elimination rule and the use case.
Semantic definition (on grammars):

i.e. there exists a decomposition w = u_1 \cdot w' \cdot u_2 with at least one of u_1, u_2 non-empty, and A holds on w'. (The two summands handle "left margin non-empty" and "right margin non-empty"; their overlap is also non-empty on both sides, which is fine since \oplus of A-witnesses is just "either witness".)
Elimination rule, by analogy with ▷-app-NE:

Fixed-point principle: \mathsf {lob}_\mathrm {sub} : (\triangleright _\mathrm {sub}\, A \vdash A) \to (\top \vdash A). Well-foundedness comes from |w'| < |w| whenever w = u_1 \cdot w' \cdot u_2 and one of u_1, u_2 is non-empty.

html:ul.html:li: Bracketed-content recursion without staging. Currently the parens parser consumes \langle , recurses on the suffix, then checks the inner leftover for \rangle . With \triangleright _\mathrm {sub}, we could directly recurse on "the content between \langle and \rangle " once we've found the matching close — a much more natural decomposition.

Dyck and similar grammars. The inner D in \langle D \rangle D is a proper substring of the outer input, not a suffix. With \triangleright _\mathrm {sub} we'd express this directly rather than via the suffix-and-leftover dance. See item 7.

Left-associative iteration. Reframe a left-assoc operator loop as: parse an atom a_n at the end of the input, recurse on the substring "everything before a_n" to get a_1 \, \mathit {op} \, \cdots \, \mathit {op} \, a_{n-1}. The recursive call is on a proper substring.
Two-sided patterns like a^n\, b\, c^n. The marker b is in the middle; recursion on the substring strictly between the two "ends" is the natural shape.

fr:title.text: 7. Dyck as a guarded fixed point

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: 7. Dyck as a guarded fixed point

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Cass's intuition (per discussion): the Dyck grammar can be described not just as the initial algebra \mu (I \oplus \langle \, X\, \rangle \, X) but as a guarded fixed point of a functor that turns "later grammars" into "current grammars" by consuming brackets.
Concretely:
The question marks are exactly the elimination of \triangleright _?: each occurrence of X is consumed at a position where the input has already given up at least one character. Two Xs appear:

html:ul.html:li: The inner X matches the contents between \langle and \rangle . Its input is a proper substring of the parent input (margins \langle and \rangle ++ \cdots on either side, both non-empty). Naturally a use of \triangleright _\mathrm {sub}.
The outer X matches the suffix after the closing \rangle . Its input is a proper suffix of the parent input. A use of \triangleright (left-handed).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: So the modality at the recursive position is a sort of join: either \triangleright or \triangleright _\mathrm {sub} suffices to witness productivity. One could take \triangleright _\mathrm {join} as the disjunction (a third modality), or use a heterogeneous functor where each X position is annotated with its own modality.

Connection to well-foundedness. The \mu -view of Dyck is the initial algebra of a polynomial functor; well-foundedness comes from structural induction on the inductive type. The guarded view gives an alternative justification: the unique fixed point under productivity. Both views coincide because Dyck is unambiguous — every Dyck word has exactly one parse tree.
Guarded fixed-point operator on grammars. The required primitive is

such that \mathsf {gfix}\, F \cong F(\mathrm {next}(\mathsf {gfix}\,F)) as grammars. This is the grammar-level analogue of lob (which operates at the term level on parser combinators). With it, Dyck = gfix DyckF, and we'd have a clean equivalence Dyck ≅ μ DyckBaseFunctor to relate the two encodings.

Payoff. Importing guarded-type-theory technology (clock variables, ticks, Iris-style modal reasoning) to grammars. Useful for: equivalences between \mu and \mathsf {gfix} definitions; modular productivity proofs that compose; semantic accounts of non-well-founded grammar definitions (e.g. infinite-arity \oplus _d where the index set itself is given by a guarded process).

fr:title.text: Recursive descent parsers in the dependent Lambek calculus

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Recursive descent parsers in the dependent Lambek calculus

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Notes on building small recursive descent parsers on top of the combinator library in Grammar.Parser, where recursion is encoded by Löb induction on the left-handed later modality \triangleright . Each parser is a closed term \mathtt {string} \vdash \mathsf {Maybe}\, A that reduces concretely on small inputs, so successful typechecking of refl-style tests is the evidence that the parser produces the right answer. Companion to sss-00BT (Chu / parser-combinator vocabulary) and to the ▷-modality construction in sss-00B9.

The DSL combinators (\otimes , \oplus , \triangleright -app, …) are mostly opaque, so reducing \mathtt {string} \vdash \mathsf {Maybe}\, A on a concrete word requires unfolding every primitive at the test site. Grammar.Parser.Eval bundles all the relevant unfoldings under a single marker eval-parser : Unit; a test file then writes
and inherits the entire chain transitively — Agda 2.9's unfolding is transitive through markers, so one local name buys access to dozens of opaques scattered across Grammar.*.
File: src/Examples/ArithRDLater.agda. Grammar

recognized by parseP = fixP step with step of type \triangleright A_0 \vdash A_0 dispatching on the first character of the input. The a-case consumes one character and recurses on the suffix via ▷-app-NE-keep-⌈⌉ aNE; the empty and +-cases emit NIL with the input left intact as leftover.

Tests in Examples/ArithRDLaterTests.agda: five refl-based assertions on a Bool-valued acceptAStr, mirroring the accept? trick from Examples/Benchmark/Dyck.agda. Witness-level reduction is expensive enough — even with all opaques unfolded — that we sidestep it pending a later performance investigation.
File: src/Examples/ArithParensRDLater.agda. Grammar

adding bracket tokens to the alphabet. The new open-bracket case projects \triangleright A_0 at the singleton prefix consisting of one open bracket, getting an inner parser result, then peeks at the inner leftover for a close bracket (via bindP) before constructing PARENSP. Inner failure or a missing close bracket both fail the whole branch.

Twelve refl-based acceptance tests in Examples/ArithParensRDLaterTests.agda cover nested parens, prefix-a^\ast sequences, and three failure cases (unmatched open, lone close, and trailing a after a closed group).
The simple template fixes a single static prefix per recursive call. Handling BinOp's grammar
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: E \;\;:=\;\; A \;\;\mid \;\; A + E, \qquad A \;\;:=\;\; n \;\;\mid \;\; \langle E \rangle
fr:mainmatter.html:p: from Examples.BinOp.LL⟨1⟩ bumps into this: after parsing a bracketed expression we would need to recurse again on a runtime-determined suffix to consume a possible + E, but ▷-app-NE-keep-⌈⌉ only projects \triangleright A_0 at a prefix we name statically. Two ways out:

html:ul.html:li: Duplicate \triangleright A_0 via the diagonal and use ▷-app-NE (the non-\lceil \cdot \rceil variant) with an ad-hoc NonEmpty proof for the bracketed prefix. Mechanically fine, but the proof obligation pollutes the parser body.

Use a different fixpoint shape that iterates rather than only recurses on the suffix. Pratt parsing is the canonical version: parseExp(minPrec) consumes an atom, then loops while the next operator's left binding power exceeds minPrec, with the operator's right binding power passed back into the recursive call. The loop body consumes a runtime-determined prefix per iteration (atom · op · atom · …), so the static-prefix restriction shows up as the central design problem rather than an asymmetry.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We take the second route below, but observe that the static-prefix restriction can be accommodated rather than overcome: every recursion site in a Pratt-style body consumes a 2-token prefix atom · op that is statically known after dispatching on those two tokens via \oplus ^\mathsf {d}-elim. The right-associative case becomes a one-pass Löb induction with prefix \lceil \mathit {atom}, \mathit {op} \rceil at each step.
File: src/Examples/PrattRDLater.agda. Grammar
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: E \;\;:=\;\; A \;\;\mid \;\; A + E, \qquad A \;\;:=\;\; a \;\;\mid \;\; \langle E \rangle
fr:mainmatter.html:p: with + right-associative. A single recursive parser via fixP. The body dispatches on the first character of the input:

html:ul.html:li: \langle : recurse to parse the inner E (project \triangleright A_0 at the singleton prefix \lceil \langle \rceil ), then peek the inner parser's leftover for \rangle via bindP, then build the PARENS node.

a: peek the next character. If it is +, project \triangleright A_0 at the two-character prefix \lceil a, +\rceil , parse the rhs E on the suffix, and combine into a PLUS node. Otherwise return the bare atom and leave whatever follows as the leftover.
anything else: fail.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The 2-character static prefix \lceil a, +\rceil gives every operator-recursion site a known static prefix atom-token · op-token, exactly the input shape that ▷-app-NE-keep-⌈⌉ can project. Eleven refl-based acceptance tests in Examples/PrattRDLaterTests.agda cover right-associated chains, paren groups, mixed sequences, and four failure cases (lone op, dangling op, op-leading, trailing atom).
File: src/Examples/PrattRDLaterGen.agda. A module Build parameterised by a record
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: record PrattSpec : Type₁ where field AI : Type ℓ-zero -- atom token indices isSetAI : isSet AI OI : Type ℓ-zero -- operator token indices isSetOI : isSet OI
fr:mainmatter.html:p: with alphabet \mathit {AI} \uplus \mathit {OI}. The grammar

has \mathsf {Atom} = \bigoplus _{a \in \mathit {AI}} \mathsf {literal}\,a and \mathsf {Op} = \bigoplus _{o \in \mathit {OI}} \mathsf {literal}\,o. The parser body dispatches on (i) the first character via the \uplus -structure of the alphabet, then (ii) inside the atom branch, on the second character. Each (atom, op) pair has its own static 2-token prefix, named uniformly in a, o.

Adding an operator is a one-line change to the OI datatype at the instantiation site — the parser body and proofs are untouched. Concrete tests in Examples/PrattRDLaterGenTests.agda instantiate with atoms \{a, b\} and operators \{+, *\}, ten refl-based assertions covering atom sequences, mixed-op chains, and failure cases.

fr:title.text: Where this stops: precedence and fixity

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Where this stops: precedence and fixity

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two extensions are still open:

html:ul.html:li: Multiple precedence levels. The current grammar has one level, so it accepts a * b + c as a * (b + c) — the operator order in the input determines the tree, not the operators' precedences. A stratified grammar E_n := E_{n-1} \mid E_{n-1}\, op_n\, E_n per level would fix this, with the parser becoming either a finite tuple of Löb-fixed mutually recursive parsers or a single parser whose state is a level index.

Left-associative operators. The current parser is single-pass right-associative because the recursion shape is [atom, op] · rhs. Left-associativity needs iteration with an accumulator, i.e. the loop body consumes one op · atom step on a left context that grows by accumulation. In the Löb-induction fixpoint shape, this is the runtime-prefix scenario discussed above: either an ad-hoc ▷-app-NE use or a different fixpoint, e.g. fixPr (right-handed) so that the recursive call consumes the final atom and the head accumulator is the runtime-shaped prefix.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pratt's classical single parser with an explicit minPrec parameter unifies both: at each step it consumes one op only if \mathit {lbp}(\mathit {op}) > \mathit {minPrec}, and recurses with \mathit {rbp}(\mathit {op}) (which equals \mathit {lbp} for left-assoc, \mathit {lbp}-1 for right-assoc). Encoding this in our setting wants a Löb fix on the precedence-indexed family \triangleright (\forall p.\, \mathsf {Parser}\,E) \vdash \forall p.\, \mathsf {Parser}\,E. The static-prefix restriction is no longer the obstacle — the open question is the cleanest way to thread the runtime precedence through the recursive call. Punted to a follow-up.

fr:title.text: Atkey's reduct as a recursive-coalgebra / corecursive-algebra stack

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Atkey's reduct as a recursive-coalgebra / corecursive-algebra stack

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Synthesis tying Atkey's data types with negation and the GL-reduct route to complement grammars to the recursive-coalgebra framework of [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint] that underwrites the derivative-based CFG parser plan and Cass's claim that (\mu F)^{-1} is always recursive.

The Cass–Urbat–Wißmann picture: an intrinsically correct algorithm is the unique c2a-morphism from a recursive coalgebra (C, \gamma : C \to FC) to an algebra (A, \alpha : FA \to A). For a parser, the algebra is \mu F^+ and the coalgebra is the input string with derivative structure. Parse is intrinsically correct because it is unique. This is a purely positive story.
Atkey's reduct is the bilateral generalisation. The doubled fixed point
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: D \;=\; \mu ^i Y.\;{\mathopen {}\left (\mu X^+.\, F^+(X^+, Y^-),\;\nu X^-.\, F^-(Y^+, X^-)\right )\mathclose {}}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: forces a \mu on the positive side and a \nu on the negative side. The two sides have dual recursion principles, which already exist in the literature as the two halves of Capretta–Uustalu– Vene:

html:ul.html:li: Positive. Initial algebra \mu F^+; recursion principle is recursive coalgebra (CUV 2006). Style: catamorphism / fold / well-founded. Computes a parse tree.
Negative. Terminal coalgebra \nu F^-; recursion principle is corecursive algebra (CUV 2009). Style: anamorphism / unfold / productive. Computes a refutation trace.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: So the reduct is a recursive-coalgebra / corecursive-algebra bialgebraic construction, doubly nested: an outer \mu ^i in \mathbf {Chu}^i parameterising an inner \mu on the positive side and an inner \nu on the negative side. Each layer has a known universal property. None of this is new — what is new is that putting them together gives complement grammars under recursion.
Cass's claim: the inverse of an initial algebra is always a recursive coalgebra, regardless of whether it is the final coalgebra. Apply it twice in the reduct stack:

html:ul.html:li: Inner positive. D^+ = \mu X^+.\, F^+(X^+, Y^-) (with Y^- fixed) is an initial algebra. Its inverse is recursive \Rightarrow structural recursion on parse trees works without step-indexing or guarded modalities.

Outer \mu ^i. The outer fixed point is an initial algebra in \mathbf {Chu}^i. By the same lemma — lifted to \mathbf {Chu}^i, which needs a separate check — its inverse is recursive \Rightarrow recursion on the stage of knowledge Y is well-founded.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Dually, the standard CUV theorem the inverse of a terminal coalgebra is a corecursive algebra fires on the negative side, giving productivity for refutation generation. So the negative half also avoids guarded modalities, again contingent on the lemma transporting to our setting.

fr:title.text: Lambek connectives in Chu over Grammar

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Lambek connectives in Chu over Grammar

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Each connective on Grammar lifts to Chu pairs by separating positive evidence from negative evidence:

The first two rows are the Cartesian product and coproduct of \mathbf {Chu}(\mathbf {Gr}, \mathrel {\And }, \bot ) — forced by the construction, with negation flipping coordinates. This block is the symmetric *-autonomous Chu category Atkey works in, transported from (\mathbf {Set}, \times , \emptyset ) to our setting.

The middle two rows lift the Lambek tensor \otimes and its pointwise De Morgan dual (A \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} B)(w) = \forall \text { splits } w_1 w_2 = w.\; A(w_1) \oplus B(w_2) to Chu pairs by symmetric pattern matching: positive on positive, dual on dual. These are not the symmetric Chu tensor — they encode a separate non-commutative Lambek monoidal structure on Chu pairs, which is what actual grammars use.

Unit of \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}. The grammar \mathsf {NES}(w) = (w 
eq \varepsilon ) is a unit for \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}: for w 
eq \varepsilon , every split has either w_1 
eq \varepsilon (making NES hold) or w_1 = \varepsilon (making the A branch fire); for w = \varepsilon , only the trivial split exists and A(\varepsilon ) is required. So the Lambek unit lifts to \varepsilon \mapsto (\varepsilon ,\, \mathsf {NES}).

Caveat — Grammar is not *-autonomous. A^{**} \neq A because A \multimap \bot collapses (the linear function space into \bot kills variation in A). So \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} on Grammar gets a unit but (\otimes , \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}, \varepsilon , \mathsf {NES}) is not a self-dual closed structure on Grammar itself. Duality lives at the Chu level — the Chu-consistency condition A^+ \mathrel {\And } A^- \vdash \bot is what makes the lifted operations well-typed in the first place.

Atomic lifts. A character c lifts to (\mathsf {lit}(c),\, \neg \mathsf {lit}(c)) where \neg \mathsf {lit}(c) is the ordinary grammar "any string distinct from a single character c". The recursion variable X lifts to (X^+, X^-). Pointwise disjointness holds for each lift by construction.

Strictly positive functor separation. A strictly positive recursive grammar F(X) uses only the connectives in the table with X appearing positively, and so lifts to a Chu functor F(X^+, X^-) = (F^+(X^+, X^-),\, F^-(X^+, X^-)) by walking the syntax. When F contains no negation, the lift specialises further — F^+ depends only on X^+ and F^- only on X^- — so the doubled fixed point
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: D \;=\; \mu ^i Y.\; {\mathopen {}\left (\mu X^+.\, F^+(X^+, Y^-),\;\nu X^-.\, F^-(Y^+, X^-)\right )\mathclose {}}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: collapses to two independent inner fixed points and the outer \mu ^i becomes trivial. For finite-string grammars where the negative recursion is well-founded by string length, the inner \nu agrees with \mu .

fr:title.text: What we need in the codebase

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What we need in the codebase

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Four pieces, in order of independence:

html:ul.html:li: Final coalgebras. The reduct uses \nu on the refutation side, and we currently have only \mu (Grammar.Inductive.Indexed, Kleene star). The user has implemented terminal coalgebras for indexed containers in this codebase before and deleted that work; restoring it is the prerequisite for everything else here. The construction is not research — it is library work.

Chu-over-Grammar as a defined category. A record \mathsf {ChuG} = (A^+ : \mathbf {Gr}) \times (A^- : \mathbf {Gr}) \times (A^+ \mathrel {\And } A^- \vdash \bot ). The pairing uses \mathrel {\And } (Cartesian product on \mathbf {Gr}), not \otimes (Lambek concatenation): A^+ \mathrel {\And } A^- \vdash \bot unfolds to \forall w.\, \neg (A^+(w) \times A^-(w)), the pointwise disjointness condition that already lives in our Parser record. The pairing A^+ \otimes A^- \vdash \bot is a different — and degenerate — condition: it unfolds to \forall w_1\, w_2.\, \neg (A^+(w_1) \times A^-(w_2)), which forces one of A^\pm to be everywhere empty (concatenation is total in the free monoid). So Chu over (\mathrel {\And }, \bot ) is the construction we want; Chu over (\otimes , \bot ) kills all non-trivial pairs. Since \mathrel {\And } is Cartesian, \mathsf {ChuG} is a symmetric *-autonomous category by the standard recipe — no Barr-style non-commutative machinery needed.

Show our Parser factors through Chu. Parser A B should become ChuG (A, B) together with a totality witness \StringGram \vdash A \oplus B. The wk-eqv-parse lemma transports along weak equivalence in the positive coordinate; verify it factors through the Chu morphism structure.

The reduct theorem. A polynomial-functor language for grammars-with-complement, with the doubled-fixed-point initial-algebra theorem proven in our setting. Atkey works in (\mathbf {Set}, \times , \emptyset ); we work in (\mathbf {Gr}, \mathrel {\And }, \bot ). The reduct argument is generic over a Cartesian closed base, and \mathbf {Gr} is Cartesian closed under \mathrel {\And }, so transcription is mostly mechanical once \nu is back in the library. The non-commutative \otimes does not enter the *-autonomous structure of ChuG — it appears only as content inside the polynomial functors F^\pm that describe recursive grammars.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What's in the literature. de Paiva (2018) and de Paiva, Eades & Jiang (2019) construct Dialectica-style models of Lambek directly, using the non-commutative \otimes . Dialectica is a refinement of Chu — it adds a relation between A^+ and A^- rather than a pairing into a fixed dualiser — and they choose to put the non-commutativity in the Chu/Dialectica structure itself. Our choice above is different: we keep the *-autonomous structure symmetric (over \mathrel {\And }) and let the non-commutative \otimes appear inside positive and negative grammars rather than between them. Both choices are defensible; ours is closer to Atkey's Set-based template. Barr (1995) is the relevant reference for the alternative route — Chu over a biclosed non-commutative tensor with two implications. We do not currently need it, but it is what would be required to put \otimes into the Chu structure should that turn out to matter for some application (e.g. a non-commutative Chu where the two implications model directional parsing strategies). Neither de Paiva paper nor the slides develop the formal-language / parser-totality side; that gap is what the synthesis tree and the present tree address.

Decidability/totality is the orthogonal concern. The reduct gives us a Chu pair (D^+, D^-) with consistency for free; whether the resulting (D^+, D^-) is total (i.e. yields a Parser) remains a separate theorem. For Dyck this is just the statement that Dyck is a DCFL, which is true.
Once \mathsf {ChuG} is in place we get a *-autonomous category over our grammar SMC for free, with a linear negation (A^+, A^-)^* = (A^-, A^+) and a par. Two things this opens up:

html:ul.html:li: Coinductive parsing. The same \nu that powers the reduct lets us write streaming/online parsers and parsers for non-well-founded languages directly. The user already had ▷-style work in sss-00BE and sss-00B9; reviving final coalgebras dovetails with that.

PEG-style negative lookahead as a primitive grammar. With the reduct in place, a former !A (anything but A) can be a primitive grammar with denotational semantics, instead of an operational hack. This is the application Atkey originally sells the construction on.

Atkey works in \mathbf {Set} with \times ; we work in \mathbf {Gr} with \mathrel {\And }. Both are Cartesian closed, so the *-autonomous Chu structure transports without extra work. The non-commutative \otimes on \mathbf {Gr} is content inside the recursive functors F^\pm , not part of the Chu structure.

We require totality (string parses as either A^+ or A^-). Atkey does not, and his examples \mathsf {Liar} \cong (\bot ,\bot ) and \mathsf {NoBaseCase} \cong (\bot , \top ) require this slack. Our totalising specialisation forbids them, which is correct for parsers.
No formal-language-theoretic development in the slides — closure, decidability, and grammar-theoretic results are all on us.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The diagram chase does not go through for arbitrary grammars — the verification check anticipated above fails. next is not derivable from the indexed-product definition of ▷ alone; it requires extra structure on A.

Max's framing. Presheaves on (\texttt {String}, \text {suffix-order}) are precisely \Box -coalgebras over families. The map next : A ⊢ ▷ A is the coalgebra structure, not a global term. So instead of postulating it (or holding it open as a hole), package it as a record:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: record IsCoalgebra (A : Grammar ℓA) : Type ℓA where field next : A ⊢ ▷ A
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The canonical example is ⊤-IsCoalgebra: ⊤ is suffix-closed because any suffix of a ⊤-parse is a ⊤-parse. This lives in Grammar/Later/Coalgebra.agda on the guarded branch of gsa-brzozowski.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The plan is self-contained without any modalities: productivity is a side condition on CFGDesc, nullability is an external decision sss-00A5, and well-foundedness is operational recursion on length sss-00A8. A later operator ▶ would internalise each of these into the type system, making the same construction fall out of guarded fixpoint rather than a sequence of external theorems.
Two natural slots for ▶:

html:p.html:strong: 1. As the guard on μ in CFGDesc.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The current productivity condition on CFGDesc ("every self-reference sits under a non-nullable prefix") is a bespoke later modality indexed by "must consume ≥1 char." First-class ▶ replaces the side condition with a syntactic requirement:

where F is any unconstrained CFGDesc-style functor. This is exactly the trade-up that the Grammar.SequentialUnambiguity.Nullable scaffolding already gestures at: ¬Nullable A is a proposition about a grammar; ▶ would be a grammar constructor.

The paper's guard functor (F ↓₀) X i = F (λ j → (j ≺ i) × X j) i is already a parameterised later modality: the parameter is the well-founded relation ≺, not a global clock. So the machinery in IntrinsicallyRecursiveCoalgs.lagda is morally a per-index ▶, and moving to a syntactic ▶ is just factoring that indexing into the type theory.

html:p.html:strong: 2. As the meaning of A ⟜ char c.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Recall from ⟜-as-derivative that
(A ⟜ char c) w = A (c ∷ w),

i.e. inhabiting A ⟜ char c requires being fed one character before producing an A. This is the defining behaviour of a later modality: availability delayed by one step, where "step" = "one character consumed."
Under this reading the Brzozowski identity char c · A ≅ δ c A becomes an applicativity law:
char c · (A ⟜ char c) ⊢ A (▶-apply)
and the derivative-based parser is a guarded fixpoint:

html:p.html:code: parse : μ self. (char? ⟜ ε ⊕ (Σ c. ▶ (parse (δ c G))))

fr:mainmatter.html:p: where the self-reference is guarded by ▶ ≡ (_ ⟜ char c), and the well-foundedness witness F-ε⁻¹ of c2a-morph is exactly the "take a later and cash it in" rule.

c2a-morph becomes guarded fixpoint. The paper's uniqueness theorem specialises to the Löb-style uniqueness of guarded fixpoints in the appropriate topos. Computational content is the same; meta-theory is cleaner.

Which ▶? Classical guarded type theory's ▶ is character-agnostic (one "tick" per step). Ours is character-indexed (▶_c A = A ⟜ char c). The paper's (F ↓₀) sits in between — indexed by an abstract ≺. Whether to use a single ▶ or a character-indexed family is itself a design question.

fr:title.text: Parser by Well-Founded Recursion on String Length

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Parser by Well-Founded Recursion on String Length

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We want a generic parser
for every G : CFGDesc, where Parser A B (from Parser.Base) packages a splitting string ⊢ A ⊕ B with a disjointness witness disjoint A B.
Construction, by induction on input length:

html:ol.html:li: If the input is ε, answer by decidable nullability: G is nullable ⟹ inhabit ⟦ G ⟧cfg, otherwise inhabit the rejection side.

If the input is c ∷ w, recursively parse (δ c G) w via the syntactic derivative. Using ⟜ as derivative, a positive answer ⟦ δ c G ⟧cfg w reshapes to ⟦ G ⟧cfg (c ∷ w); a negative answer ¬ ⟦ δ c G ⟧cfg w lifts to ¬ ⟦ G ⟧cfg (c ∷ w).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Well-foundedness: on each recursive call length w strictly decreases. The grammar may grow (derivatives of CFGs are unbounded), but the well-founded relation is on the input, not the state. This mirrors how GCD.<₂-wellFounded in the intrinsically-recursive paper is well-founded on proj₂ of the index, not on the full index.
Concretely, the recursion uses <-wellFounded on ℕ via Cubical.Induction.WellFounded (already imported by the project's dependency on agda-stdlib).

This tree defines the algorithm operationally. The next step, parser as c2a-morphism, reinterprets the same definition as a unique coalgebra-to-algebra morphism, so the correctness proof becomes a uniqueness argument rather than a direct induction.
Milestone: implement this first for a hand-rolled Dyck (bypassing CFGDesc for the moment) to shake out the ⟜/nullability gymnastics before trying to generalise.
In Grammar.LinearFunction.Base, the right residual is (A ⟜ B) w = ∀ (w' : String) → B w' → A (w' ++ w). Reading this at a single-character grammar char c we get
(G ⟜ char c) w = ∀ w' → (char c) w' → G (w' ++ w) ≅ G (c ∷ w),
i.e. the Brzozowski derivative of G by c, up to the canonical iso char c · w ≅ c ∷ w for singleton matches.

So the calculus already has a semantic notion of derivative as a type constructor, not just as an operation on descriptions. The syntactic derivative δ c G should then denote exactly ⟦ G ⟧cfg ⟜ char c, and the Brzozowski adjointness c · G ≅ δ c G is an instance of the tensor/residual adjunction char c · G ⊢ H ⟺ G ⊢ H ⟜ char c.
Why this matters for the plan:

html:ul.html:li: It grounds δ in the calculus rather than treating it as an external device: δ c G = G ⟜ char c already has the right type.
It means the parser's recursive structure can be phrased internally as currying over char c · - / uncurrying over - ⟜ char c, without leaving the calculus.
It suggests CFGDesc may not need ⟜ as a primitive — the operator can live outside the description as long as we can compute δ on descriptions and prove ⟦ δ c G ⟧cfg ≅ ⟦ G ⟧cfg ⟜ char c.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Open question: for grammars with nullable residuals the adjunction interacts with the nullability gating in δ c (G · H); make sure the semantic direction of the iso stays available in both cases. This is tracked in risks.
